options.text: An IDE plugin that runs tests locally
options.explanation: Runner runs on a server or VM, not in an IDE.

options.text: A web interface for viewing GitLab pipelines
options.explanation: The web interface is GitLab itself. Runner is a separate agent.

options.text: An agent that receives tasks from GitLab and executes them on the machine where it is installed
options.explanation: GitLab Runner is a separate program (agent) that polls GitLab, picks up jobs, and executes them.

options.text: A Docker image with pre-installed GitLab
options.explanation: GitLab and GitLab Runner are different programs. Runner is the execution agent.

question: Your job has tags [docker, linux, arm64]. Which runner will take this job?

options.text: A runner with tags [docker, linux, arm64, ci]
options.explanation: The runner must have all job tags. Having an extra tag ci is not a problem.

options.text: A runner with tags [linux, windows, arm64]
options.explanation: This runner lacks the docker tag — it will skip the job.

options.text: A runner with tags [docker]
options.explanation: The runner must have ALL job tags. Tags linux and arm64 are missing — it will skip.

options.text: Any available runner with run_untagged = true
options.explanation: run_untagged only applies to jobs WITHOUT tags. This job has tags, so an exact match is required.

question: What is the fundamental difference between Docker executor and Shell executor?

options.text: Shell executor does not require additional software on the host machine
options.explanation: Shell executor requires all dependencies (Node, Python, etc.) directly on the host machine.

options.text: Shell executor runs scripts directly on the host machine without isolation
options.explanation: Shell executor is the fastest, but jobs can affect each other and the system.

options.text: Docker executor runs each job in an isolated container
options.explanation: Yes, each job gets a fresh container — full isolation.

options.text: Docker executor only works with public Docker Hub images
options.explanation: Docker executor works with any images: public, private, or from your own registry.

question: What happens if no runner matches the tags for a job?

options.text: The job remains in pending status and waits for a matching runner
options.explanation: The job stays in the pending queue. If no runner appears — it times out (default 1 hour).

options.text: GitLab automatically creates a new runner
options.explanation: GitLab does not create runners automatically. An administrator must register runners in advance.

options.text: The job fails immediately with an error
options.explanation: The job does not fail immediately — it enters the queue and waits for a matching runner.

options.text: The job will be executed on any available runner
options.explanation: No, if tags don't match, the runner will not take the job — this protects against accidental execution.

question: What is a Protected Runner and why is it needed?

options.text: A runner with SSL/TLS enabled for secure connection to GitLab
options.explanation: All runners use HTTPS. Protected is about branches, not encryption.

options.text: A runner that takes jobs only from protected branches (main, release/*)
options.explanation: A protected runner does not execute jobs from regular feature branches, which protects production from malicious code.

options.text: A runner with a password for access
options.explanation: Runner access is managed via tokens, not passwords. Protected is about branch restrictions.

options.text: A runner that automatically creates backup copies of artifacts
options.explanation: This is not related to Protected runners. Protected is exclusively about restriction to protected branches.

question: Your team spends $500/month on GitLab CI minutes. You have 5 developers, pipelines run 50 times a day, each takes ~15 minutes. What's the best action?

options.text: Reduce the number of tests to make pipelines faster
options.explanation: Reducing tests is a bad trade-off. Savings should come from infrastructure, not quality.

options.text: Buy more CI minutes from GitLab
options.explanation: At this usage intensity, a self-hosted runner will pay for itself in 1-2 months.

options.text: Run pipelines only once a day on a schedule
options.explanation: This destroys the fast feedback loop — the main value of CI. Don't sacrifice practice for savings.

options.text: Set up a self-hosted runner on your own server or cloud
options.explanation: 50 runs x 15 min x 30 days = 22,500 minutes/month. Even a small VPS (~$30-50/month) is cheaper than $500.

question: Which parameters in config.toml are important for controlling parallelism?

options.text: check_interval — how often the runner polls GitLab for new jobs
options.explanation: check_interval (in seconds) affects the delay before a job starts after appearing in the queue.

options.text: concurrent — maximum number of simultaneously executing jobs
options.explanation: concurrent at the top level of the config limits the total number of parallel jobs.

options.text: max_jobs — maximum jobs over the entire runner lifetime
options.explanation: There is no such parameter in config.toml. There is MaxBuilds in the context of autoscaling (docker+machine).

options.text: timeout — wait time before taking the next job
options.explanation: timeout in job is the maximum execution time. There is no 'wait before taking' parameter.

question: When should you use Kubernetes executor instead of Docker executor?

options.text: When you need automatic scaling without additional configuration
options.explanation: Kubernetes creates new Pods under load and removes them afterward — autoscaling out of the box.

options.text: When you need precise control of CPU and Memory for each job
options.explanation: Kubernetes allows setting requests and limits on CPU/Memory for each Pod — a unique capability.

options.text: When you need maximum job start speed
options.explanation: Kubernetes Pods take longer to start than Docker containers. For start speed, Shell or Docker is better.

options.text: When the team already has a Kubernetes cluster and expertise
options.explanation: Kubernetes executor requires a configured cluster. If one already exists — it makes sense to use it for runners.

question: What does the run_untagged = true parameter mean for a runner?

options.text: The runner creates Docker containers without image tags
options.explanation: run_untagged has nothing to do with Docker image tags. It's about GitLab CI job tags.

options.text: The runner ignores job tags and takes any assignment
options.explanation: No, run_untagged does not mean ignoring tags. If a job has tags, matching is still mandatory.

options.text: The runner executes jobs that have no tags section in .gitlab-ci.yml
options.explanation: Yes, a runner with run_untagged = true takes jobs that have no tags: section at all.

options.text: The runner does not register tags for new jobs
options.explanation: This is not about registration. run_untagged = true simply allows the runner to take jobs without tags.

question: Why is it NOT recommended to use privileged = true for Docker executor without necessity?

options.text: You cannot use runner cache in privileged mode
options.explanation: Cache works independently of privileged. These are unrelated settings.

options.text: A malicious job could gain full access to the host system
options.explanation: A privileged container has access to host devices. Container compromise = host compromise.

options.text: Isolation between containers is broken
options.explanation: A privileged container can interact with other containers and bypass namespace isolation.

options.text: Job execution is slowed down by additional checks
options.explanation: privileged = true does not slow down execution. It is purely a security concern.

question: The team is setting up a runner for production deployment. Which settings are mandatory?

options.text: Assign unique tags that only this runner has
options.explanation: Unique tags (e.g., production-deploy) ensure that only the right jobs land on this runner.

options.text: Make the runner Protected (for protected branches only)
options.explanation: A protected runner guarantees that production deployment only happens from protected branches (main, release/*).

options.text: Set run_untagged = true so the runner takes all jobs
options.explanation: This is dangerous for a production runner. It should only take specially marked jobs, not everything.

options.text: Set privileged = true for maximum performance
options.explanation: privileged affects security, not performance. For production, minimal privileges is a mandatory requirement.

question: Where is the main GitLab Runner configuration file stored after installation?

options.text: /var/log/gitlab-runner.conf
options.explanation: /var/log is for logs, not configs. The runner config is in /etc/gitlab-runner/.

options.text: ~/.gitlab-runner/config.yml
options.explanation: The file is called config.toml (TOML format), not YAML. And on Linux the path is system-level, not in the home directory.

options.text: /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml
options.explanation: The standard path for a system installation on Linux — /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml.

options.text: gitlab-runner.json in the current directory
options.explanation: The runner does not look for config in the current directory. Config is in the system location /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml.

question: How does a Group runner differ from a Project runner?

options.text: A Group runner is available to all projects in the group, a Project runner — only to one project
options.explanation: This is the key difference: scope. A Group runner is registered at the group level, a Project runner at the project level.

options.text: A Project runner automatically gets all project secrets
options.explanation: Access to secrets (CI/CD Variables) is configured separately and does not depend on runner type.

options.text: A Group runner cannot be used with Docker executor
options.explanation: Executor type does not depend on runner scope. Any runner type can use any executor.

options.text: A Group runner is faster because it uses a special protocol
options.explanation: Speed does not depend on type. The difference is only in scope: which projects the runner is available to.

question: A developer sees that the 'deploy-prod' job picked a shared runner instead of the dedicated production runner. How to fix this?

options.text: Add unique tags to the deploy-prod job in .gitlab-ci.yml
options.explanation: Tags will restrict runner selection. Only a runner with those tags will take this job.

options.text: Remove shared runners from the project (disable in Settings > CI/CD)
options.explanation: You can disable shared runners for the project and use only your own — this completely solves the problem.

options.text: Make the production runner Protected and ensure deploy runs from a protected branch
options.explanation: A protected runner won't take jobs from unprotected branches, adding a protective barrier.

options.text: Set run_untagged = false on the shared runner
options.explanation: If the job has no tags, this would help. But if the job has tags that match the shared runner — it won't help.

question: Which executor is best for building projects in different languages (Node.js, Python, Go) within a single runner?

options.text: Docker executor with different images for each job
options.explanation: Each job sets image: node:20, image: python:3.12, image: golang:1.22 — ideal isolation without conflicts.

options.text: Docker Machine executor — it creates a VM for each language
options.explanation: Docker Machine is overkill for this case. It's needed for autoscaling, not for different languages.

options.text: Shell executor — it's the fastest
options.explanation: Shell would require installing Node, Python, and Go on the host machine and managing versions. This is a maintenance nightmare.

options.text: You need to register a separate runner for each language
options.explanation: This is excessive. Docker executor allows one runner to work with any language through different images.
